questions.q: What is this lesson's specific hypothesis about schema hallucination?
options: That a specific attention head attends back to the schema's column-name tokens and copies them forward, and hallucination occurs when that head fails to lock onto the right span
That every attention head in SQL Pete behaves identically
That SQL Pete never attends to the schema text at all
That hallucination is caused entirely by the choice of learning rate during RLHF
questions.explain: The hypothesis is a copying mechanism: a head that attends to the matching column name already present in the schema text and reproduces it, with hallucination occurring when that mechanism fails to engage.

questions.q: Why does this hypothesis resemble induction-head behavior from prior interpretability research?
options: Because an induction head predicts a repeated token by attending to its earlier occurrence in context, which matches reproducing a column name already present in the schema text
Because induction heads were first found in SQL-specific models
Because induction heads only exist in encoder-only models
Because induction heads and SQL generation are unrelated, so the comparison is only metaphorical
questions.explain: Induction heads attend to an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy forward what followed it — structurally similar to copying a column name that already appears in the schema text earlier in the prompt.

questions.q: Why is the induction-head literature's own evidence a reason for caution rather than confidence here?
options: Because induction heads only occur in models larger than 100B parameters
Because the research was never peer reviewed
Because induction heads have never been causally demonstrated in any model
Because the original research found strong causal evidence mainly in small attention-only models, and weaker correlational evidence in larger models with MLPs, unlike a fine-tuned 1.5B code model
questions.explain: The original induction-head work itself distinguishes strong causal evidence in small toy models from weaker correlational evidence in larger, more complex models — SQL Pete is neither a small attention-only toy model nor guaranteed to contain a clean, isolated induction head.

questions.q: How does per-head patching differ from the layer-level patching used in Lesson 22?
options: It requires no forward hooks at all
It can only be done on the embedding layer
It replaces only one attention head's contribution to a layer's output, leaving the rest of that layer's computation untouched, to isolate that head's causal effect
It patches the entire model's weights instead of one activation
questions.explain: Per-head patching narrows the intervention from an entire layer's residual stream down to a single head's slice of the attention output, isolating that head specifically rather than the whole layer.

questions.q: What would count as a positive, reportable result in this lesson's experiment?
options: The model producing any SQL query at all, regardless of correctness
A result spread evenly across every head with no standout, interpreted as strong confirming evidence
Any single head showing nonzero attention anywhere in the prompt
A specific head whose patched-in activation recovers the correct column name, combined with an attention pattern that shows it attending to the matching schema span on the correct-column run
questions.explain: A result is suggestive of the copying hypothesis only when a causal patching result (recovering the correct output) is combined with an attention pattern consistent with the copying story — not just one or the other, and not a diffuse result spread across many heads.
